name: HTV-2
source: Acton, 'Hypersonic Boost-Glide Weapons', Science & Global Security 23 (2015): 191-219, Table 3 (A-flight fit).
notes: DARPA HTV-2 waverider. Glide ballistic coefficient beta_L = 13,000 kg/m^2 (Acton: 'very similar to modern ICBM RVs' - this is NOT a low-beta vehicle). L/D = 2.6 (Acton Table 3). mass = 1000 kg (Wright, companion article). diameter_m is the FRONTAL (drag) diameter used for boost-phase reference area, NOT the planform width: Acton models the body as a flat isosceles triangle ~5 m long x ~2 m wide, but flying nose-first the frontal extent is small, so ~0.6 m is a representative frontal-equivalent. The 2 m planform / lifting behaviour is carried by glider_LD, not by this diameter. (Boost drag uses 'nose shape, widest diameter'; the slim-forebody shielding this omits was measured at ~0.01% of burnout speed for a fairing-shrouded launch - utterly dominated by propulsion (~3%) and glide-model (~3%) error, so the exact frontal value barely matters.) glider_beta_entry_kg_m2 = 17 is Acton's Eq.(8) entry beta_S for the high-AoA broadside direct-reentry phase; it is only used by the equilibrium_glide_acton mode and Acton explicitly flags his fitted beta_S (7-10) as physically unreliable (his Newtonian flat-plate estimate, Eq.22, gives >100). Default guidance here is dynamic_equilibrium_glide (gentle capture into force-balance equilibrium, no hard skip/pull-up) to model the hypothesis that HTV-2 entered gently; switch to equilibrium_glide_acton to exercise the explicit three-phase pull-up (the AHW-style entry).
